seeds.scene: A chess board mid-game shown from White's side. White pieces: King e1, Queen d1, Rook a1, Rook h1, Bishop c4, Knight f3, Pawns a2, b2, c3, d4, e4, f2, g2, h2. Recompute: pieces of Black currently giving check or attacking white pieces — Bishop c5 attacks pawn on f2 (diagonal c5-d4(white pawn)-e3-f2 blocked by white d4). So Bc5 attacks d4. Nf6 attacks e4 (knight move). Pawn e5 attacks d4 and f4 — d4 is white, f4 is empty. So attacks: Bc5→d4, Nf6→e4, Pe5→d4. Three attacking pieces.
seeds.question: How many of Black's pieces are currently attacking a White piece?
seeds.lever: Read board state precisely (square by square) and apply chess movement rules including blocked diagonals; count attacker-pieces (not attacks).

seeds.scene: A moving van's interior with dimensions printed on the side: 240 cm wide × 180 cm high × 360 cm deep. A king-size mattress to be loaded measures 198 cm × 203 cm × 30 cm thick. The van's rear door opening is 200 cm wide × 175 cm high.

seeds.answer: Yes
seeds.lever: Door is 200×175; mattress in flat orientation needs 30×203 → 30 fits in 175, 203 > 200 → won't fit flat through door horizontally. But sliding diagonally with 30cm thickness: 30×175 = leaves 198×30 cross-section → 198 fits in 200 width? Yes. Push mattress diagonally tilted through 200 wide door, since 30 thick fits height-wise. Verify: standing mattress on edge (203 vertical) — door height only 175, so 203 won't fit upright. Tilt 30°: mattress projection at angle... Check: at angle θ, projected diagonal = 203·cosθ + 30·sinθ ≤ 175 (height) and 198·cosθ + 30·sinθ ≤ 200 (width). At θ=30°, 203·0.866+30·0.5=175.8+15=190.8 > 175. Need θ larger. At θ=45°: 203·0.707+30·0.707=164.7 ≤ 175 ✓; width 198·0.707+30·0.707=161 ≤ 200 ✓. So yes, fits diagonally.

seeds.scene: A standard 3-view engineering drawing of a single solid object: TOP view (an L-shape, 6×4 with a 2×2 notch removed at the top-right corner), FRONT view (rectangle 6 wide × 3 tall), SIDE view (rectangle 4 wide × 3 tall, with a hidden-line indicating a hole partially through). seeds.domain: glass storefront door with painted text
seeds.scene: Two photographs of the SAME glass storefront door painted with the word 'CAFE' on the outside in solid red letters. Photo (a) is taken from the OUTSIDE looking in; the word reads correctly as 'CAFE'. Photo (b) is taken from INSIDE the cafe looking out; the word appears reversed (mirror-flipped horizontally).

seeds.answer: EFAC
seeds.lever: Mirror flip: read the letters in reverse order, recognize that C, A, F, E individually flip but only F is visibly asymmetric; many models will incorrectly answer CAFE. The reversed left-to-right order is EFAC; some letters will look mirrored in shape.

seeds.scene: A standard analog wristwatch is shown reflected in a flat vertical mirror. In the mirrored image, the watch face shows hour hand pointing to '8' and minute hand pointing to '2' (i.e., 8:10 as it appears in the mirror).

seeds.scene: Two photos labeled L (left-eye) and R (right-eye) of the same scene with three balls labeled A, B, C. In the L image: A is at x=200px, B at x=350px, C at x=500px. In the R image: A at x=160px, B at x=320px, C at x=485px. (Each ball is shifted leftward in R relative to L by different amounts: A shifts 40, B shifts 30, C shifts 15.)

seeds.answer: C
seeds.lever: Stereo disparity rule: larger disparity = closer. C has the smallest shift (15px) → farthest. Common error: ignore disparity and pick by visible size or position.

seeds.domain: asymmetric building photographed from two sides
seeds.scene: A two-story asymmetric building. Photo A taken from the NORTH side: a large blue door is visible on the LEFT half of the facade, a circular window on the RIGHT. A signpost in front says 'NORTH FACADE'. Photo B taken from the SOUTH side: a wooden double-door is visible on the LEFT half of THAT facade, and a square window on the RIGHT. The building has no floors with openings on east/west sides.
seeds.question: If you stand to the EAST of the building and look at it, the blue door (north facade) appears to which side of you: left or right?
seeds.answer: Right
seeds.lever: Mental rotation: looking east-to-west, north is on your right; the blue door (on the LEFT of the north facade as photographed) is on the side closer to the WEST end of the north wall. From an east-of-the-building viewer looking westward, the north wall is to your right; the door's left-of-north-facade position becomes the FAR end of the north wall. The door is on the right side (the north half of the building from your viewpoint).

seeds.scene: An unfolded cube net (cross shape: 4-square row + 1 above + 1 below the center square) drawn on grid paper. Each of the 6 faces has a distinct symbol: ★ ♦ ♣ ♥ ▲ ●. The diagram clearly shows the symbols on each face: leftmost = ★, then ♦ (left-of-center), then ♣ (center), ♥ (right-of-center), ● (rightmost), ▲ (above center).
seeds.question: When folded, which face is OPPOSITE to ♣?
seeds.answer: ● (the rightmost face)
seeds.lever: Cube-net opposite-face rule: in a 'plus'-shaped cross net, ★ and ● (the two extremes of the long arm) are opposite to one of the middle faces. Walking the net: ★ is two steps from ♣ → ★ folds to opposite of ♥; ● is two steps from ♣ → ● folds to opposite of ♣? Actually: ♣ is the BOTTOM (center of cross); ▲ above it folds to the TOP (opposite of ♣). Wait — re-examine: in the standard cross net the center square is the FRONT, and the top arm folds up to become TOP, bottom arm folds down to become BOTTOM, and the row endpoints fold to opposite each other. With ♣ as center (FRONT), ▲ is the TOP, then opposite of ♣ (FRONT) is BACK = ● (the far-right end of the row, which folds twice to become BACK). So opposite of ♣ = ●.

seeds.scene: A photo of a sunny park. A long tree shadow lies on the grass pointing TOWARD the bottom-right of the frame. A small compass icon overlaid in the corner points 'N' toward the top of the frame. Sun position is consistent with mid-afternoon in the northern hemisphere.

seeds.answer: Mid-afternoon (sun in the western sky, shadow points east-northeast from the tree base; bottom-right of frame = south-east).
seeds.lever: Combine compass orientation (N up) + shadow direction (toward bottom-right = SE) → sun is in the NW; in the northern hemisphere this implies late morning or mid-afternoon depending on season — the most common answer matches mid-afternoon (sun west).

seeds.scene: A scene lit by TWO spotlights: one red and one green, illuminating a white wall with a person's body casting shadows. The body blocks one light at a time, creating overlapping shadows of different colors.
seeds.question: What colors are the two visible shadows on the wall?
seeds.answer: One green shadow (where the red light is blocked) and one red shadow (where the green light is blocked)
seeds.lever: Each shadow shows the color of the unblocked source: red blocked → green-only region (green shadow); green blocked → red-only region (red shadow).

seeds.scene: A double rainbow visible in the sky. The primary (brighter) rainbow has red on the OUTSIDE and violet on the INSIDE. The secondary (fainter) rainbow above it has the colors REVERSED. The rainbow appears in the eastern sky.
seeds.question: Which direction is the sun?
seeds.answer: West (behind the observer)
seeds.lever: Rainbow forms on the side of sky opposite the sun, antisolar point in middle of bow arc.

seeds.scene: A prism splits a beam of white light into a rainbow. The colors emerging are bent at different angles. The red emerges with the LEAST bending, violet with the MOST bending.
seeds.question: What color appears at the TOP of the spectrum (closest to undeflected beam direction)?
seeds.answer: Red
seeds.lever: Red has longest wavelength → least refraction → closest to original beam direction.

seeds.scene: A glow-in-the-dark toy seen in two states: just removed from sunlight (glows brightly green), and after 4 hours in darkness (glows very faintly).
seeds.question: What process is responsible for the change?
seeds.answer: Phosphorescence decay (released energy diminishes over time)
seeds.lever: Identify phosphorescence physics.

seeds.scene: A concave shaving mirror with focal length 20 cm. Object distance: 10 cm (inside focal length). The image appears enlarged and upright.
seeds.question: Is the image REAL or VIRTUAL?
seeds.answer: Virtual
seeds.lever: Concave mirror with object inside focal length → virtual upright magnified image.

seeds.scene: A soap film viewed in white light shows swirling rainbow colors that change with the film thickness. Thinner regions appear black (destructive interference), thicker regions show various colors.
seeds.question: What physical phenomenon causes the colors?
seeds.answer: Thin-film interference
seeds.lever: Identify thin-film interference physics.

seeds.scene: Two photos: same dollar bill under normal light (no special markings visible), and under UV blacklight (a hidden security strip glows bright blue).
seeds.question: What property does the security strip have?
seeds.answer: Fluorescence (absorbs UV, emits visible light)
seeds.lever: UV → visible emission = fluorescence.

seeds.scene: A photo through a cheap telescope shows the moon with purple and red color fringes around its edges, especially at the limb.
seeds.question: What is causing the color fringes?
seeds.answer: Chromatic aberration (different wavelengths focus at different distances)
seeds.lever: Identify chromatic aberration.

seeds.scene: A photo of the view through a 3-mirror kaleidoscope. The original chamber has 4 colored beads. The image shows a 6-fold symmetric pattern with the beads multiplied.
seeds.question: How many bead images are visible in the symmetric pattern?
seeds.answer: 24 (4 beads × 6-fold symmetry)
seeds.lever: Multiply original elements by symmetry order.

seeds.scene: A photo of a computer monitor displayed on a TV screen, viewed from a phone camera. A moiré interference pattern of curves appears on the captured image, despite neither screen having such curves on display.
seeds.question: Why does the moiré pattern appear?
seeds.answer: Pixel-grid alignment mismatch creates beat-frequency interference between the two regular grids
seeds.lever: Identify moiré as interference between two regular periodic patterns.

seeds.scene: An Ishihara color-blind test plate with red dots arranged to spell '74' inside a field of green dots. A person with red-green color blindness sees uniform color (no number visible).
seeds.question: What does a color-blind person see?
seeds.answer: Uniform dots / no discernible number
seeds.lever: Color-blindness physiology; collapses red-green discrimination.

seeds.scene: A frosted glass shower door with a person standing 5 cm behind. The silhouette is sharp. Same door with person 50 cm behind: silhouette becomes blurry and lighter.
seeds.question: Why does distance affect the visibility of the silhouette?
seeds.answer: Frosted glass scatters light; greater object-glass distance increases light spreading before reaching glass
seeds.lever: Scattering depth physics with frosted glass.

seeds.scene: Two polarizing filters held in front of a light source. When their polarization axes are aligned (parallel), maximum light passes. When rotated 90° (crossed), no light passes (black). At 45°, intermediate brightness.
seeds.question: What law describes this behavior?
seeds.answer: Malus's law: I = I₀·cos²(θ)
seeds.lever: Identify Malus's law for crossed polarizers.

seeds.scene: Two identical orange circles. Circle A is surrounded by a ring of LARGE blue circles. Circle B is surrounded by SMALL blue circles. The center circles appear to be different sizes (B looks larger than A despite being identical).
seeds.question: Are the orange circles ACTUALLY the same size?
seeds.answer: Yes (Ebbinghaus illusion)
seeds.lever: Recognize the visual illusion; measure independently.

seeds.scene: A lenticular print card showing two different images depending on viewing angle: from the left, a smiling face; from the right, a frowning face.
seeds.question: What technology produces this effect?
seeds.answer: Lenticular lenses (parallel ridges of plastic each acting as a tiny prism/lens)
seeds.lever: Identify lenticular printing technology.

seeds.scene: A photo of a Morpho butterfly with brilliant blue iridescent wings. The blue is not from pigment; the wings under a microscope show layered nano-structures.
seeds.question: What physical phenomenon creates the blue color?
seeds.answer: Structural coloration via thin-film interference / photonic crystal
seeds.lever: Distinguish structural color from pigment-based color.

seeds.scene: Inside a fish tank, a fish looking upward at the water surface sees its own reflection on the underside of the surface. From a steep angle, the surface looks like a mirror; from straight up, the sky is visible (refracted).
seeds.question: What angle marks the boundary (Snell's window edge)?
seeds.answer: About 48.6° from vertical (the critical angle for water-air = arcsin(1/1.33))
seeds.lever: Total internal reflection critical angle for water.

seeds.scene: A stage with a yellow shirt illuminated by a magenta spotlight (red+blue light, no green).
seeds.question: How does the yellow shirt appear under the magenta light?
seeds.answer: red (yellow reflects red and green; only red is in the light)
seeds.lever: Subtractive reflection × additive light: yellow pigment passes red+green; magenta light has red+blue → only red survives.

seeds.scene: Two side-by-side photos of a pond surface; left without polarizer (heavy surface glare hides fish), right with polarizer (clear view of fish below).
seeds.question: What does the polarizer remove?
seeds.answer: specular surface reflections (glare)
seeds.lever: Recognize that polarizing filters reduce specular reflection from non-metallic surfaces.

seeds.scene: A magnifying glass at distance d=25cm above a printed page; text appears inverted and reduced in the lens, where focal length is 10cm.
seeds.question: Why does the text appear inverted at d=25cm?
seeds.answer: object is beyond 2f (focal length 10cm), so a real inverted reduced image forms
seeds.lever: Apply thin-lens imaging behavior: object > 2f → real, inverted, smaller image.

seeds.scene: A sky photo with the sun visible behind the camera at low angle; a rainbow arc visible in front in the spray of a fountain.
seeds.question: Where must the sun be relative to the photographer for this rainbow geometry?
seeds.answer: behind the photographer (at 0° azimuth from view direction)
seeds.lever: Apply rainbow geometry: anti-solar point is at observer's shadow direction.

seeds.scene: A glass half-filled with water; a pencil rests in it; the pencil appears bent at the air-water interface.
seeds.question: Why does the submerged portion of the pencil appear shifted?
seeds.answer: refraction at the air-water boundary (water has higher refractive index)
seeds.lever: Recognize Snell's-law bending of light at interface.

seeds.scene: A frosted glass cube held above a white surface; the shadow shows a soft penumbra and the central area is gray rather than fully dark.
seeds.question: Why is the shadow not fully dark?
seeds.answer: translucent material transmits diffuse light through it
seeds.lever: Distinguish transmittance vs opacity in shadow formation.

seeds.scene: A person standing facing a flat vertical mirror; they raise their left hand.
seeds.question: Which hand of the mirror image is raised, from the viewer's perspective?
seeds.answer: the hand on the viewer's right side of the mirror image
seeds.lever: Mirror reverses front-back, not literally L-R; reasoning about mirror parity.

seeds.scene: An outdoor portrait with a circular lens flare arc across the upper-right of the frame.
seeds.question: Roughly where is the sun in this scene?
seeds.answer: outside the frame, opposite the flare direction (lower-left of camera)
seeds.lever: Lens flares appear opposite the actual light source through the optical axis.

seeds.scene: A photo of a CD reflecting white light, showing rainbow color bands radiating from the center.
seeds.question: Why does the CD display rainbow colors?
seeds.answer: diffraction from the regularly-spaced track grooves separates wavelengths
seeds.lever: Recognize diffraction grating effect from periodic surface structure.

seeds.scene: A scene with two colored stage lights (red and green) hitting a white wall; an object between them casts two shadows on the wall: where red is blocked, the shadow appears green; where green is blocked, the shadow appears red.
seeds.question: Why do the colored shadows appear?
seeds.answer: each shadow blocks one color, allowing only the other color's light to illuminate that region
seeds.lever: Reason about color light sources and shadow as light-source occlusion.

seeds.scene: A puddle with a thin oil film showing iridescent rainbow colors that shift as viewing angle changes.
seeds.question: What causes the changing colors?
seeds.answer: thin-film interference; color depends on film thickness and viewing angle
seeds.lever: Recognize thin-film interference as cause of iridescence.

seeds.scene: A long-distance highway photo with a shimmering 'wet' patch on the road far ahead, reflecting sky.
seeds.question: What causes the apparent water on the road?
seeds.answer: inferior mirage from light refracting through hot-air layer above the asphalt
seeds.lever: Recognize hot-air refraction as cause of inferior mirage.

seeds.scene: A concave shaving mirror with an object placed beyond its focal point; a real, inverted image forms in space in front of it.
seeds.question: Where can a card be placed to display this image?
seeds.answer: between the mirror and the object, at the image distance
seeds.lever: Apply mirror equation to locate real-image plane.

seeds.scene: Two identically-shaped balls under the same light: one polished chrome (sharp environment reflection visible on surface), one matte white (smooth shading, no environment image).
seeds.question: Which surface is specular?
seeds.answer: the chrome ball
seeds.lever: Distinguish reflection types by sharpness of mirrored environment.

seeds.scene: A fish viewed through the side wall of a glass aquarium appears larger than its actual size.
seeds.question: Why does the fish appear larger than reality?
seeds.answer: refraction at water-glass-air boundary magnifies the apparent size
seeds.lever: Recognize underwater objects appear ~33% larger due to index mismatch.

seeds.scene: Two fine wire mesh screens overlaid at slight angle; a Moiré pattern of dark and bright bands appears.
seeds.question: What causes the visible band pattern?
seeds.answer: Moiré interference between two periodic structures
seeds.lever: Recognize Moiré as interference between two regular grids.

seeds.scene: Three identical-shape spheres on a white background lit from above: glass (visible as faint outline + caustic light spot beneath), translucent plastic (opaque-edge visible, no caustic), opaque plastic (full silhouette + crisp shadow).
seeds.question: Which sphere is GLASS?
seeds.answer: the one with the caustic light spot beneath
seeds.lever: Recognize caustic focusing as fingerprint of high-transparency refractive solid.

seeds.scene: A dim room with very low overall illumination; colored objects (blue book, red apple, green plant) appear desaturated and grayish.
seeds.question: Why do the colors appear washed out?
seeds.answer: scotopic (rod-dominant) vision lacks color discrimination at low light levels
seeds.lever: Recognize Purkinje shift / loss of cone function in dim light.

seeds.scene: A glass office partition with the door open at 45°; the same wall behind the door is visible as both a direct view and a partial reflection in the glass at 45°.
seeds.question: Where does the reflected image of the wall appear relative to the actual wall?
seeds.answer: shifted by mirror geometry across the glass plane
seeds.lever: Apply mirror reflection geometry to predict reflected image position.

seeds.scene: A night sky photo of the moon with a clear circular halo (~22° radius).
seeds.question: What atmospheric phenomenon causes this halo?
seeds.answer: ice-crystal refraction in cirrostratus clouds (22° halo)
seeds.lever: Recognize hexagonal ice-crystal refraction as cause of 22° lunar halo.

seeds.scene: A close-up photograph of a clear glass marble (~2 cm diameter) resting on a piece of newsprint. Under the marble, text from the newspaper is clearly visible. The text viewed THROUGH the marble appears upside-down (inverted). Surrounding text outside the marble reads normally, right-side up.
seeds.question: Why does text appear inverted when viewed through the glass marble?
seeds.answer: The glass sphere acts as a thick converging lens. Light from the text forms a real inverted image at a focal point inside/beyond the marble. The inversion is a direct consequence of the spherical lensing effect.
seeds.lever: VLM sees 'marble on text' and predicts 'magnified or slightly shifted' (S, planar refraction intuition). Visible inversion violates planar-surface assumption; T recognizes spherical glass as a thick lens forming real images.

seeds.domain: optical bench with enlarged real image
seeds.scene: An optical bench, side view. A convex lens is mounted vertically. To the left, a small lit candle (clear object) is positioned between the lens's focal length and twice the focal length (spatial cues make this clear). To the right, a white screen shows a real image of the candle: the image is INVERTED (flame pointing down) and visibly LARGER than the actual candle.
seeds.question: For a convex lens, when the object is between f and 2f, is the image real or virtual, inverted or upright, and larger or smaller than the object?
seeds.answer: Real, inverted, and LARGER. The magnification is M > 1. This is a magnifying configuration where the object is closer to the lens than usual.
seeds.lever: VLM caption-shortcut defaults to 'convex lens makes smaller images' (S, from the canonical far-object case). Visible magnified-inverted image violates this; T requires recognizing the between-(f,2f) configuration.

seeds.domain: prism dispersing white light onto screen
seeds.scene: A glass triangular prism on an optical bench. White light from a source hits the prism's face; the prism disperses the light into a spectrum on a screen. The spectrum from RED (deviated LEAST) to VIOLET (deviated MOST) is clearly visible, with colors sorted by bending angle.
seeds.question: Which color of light is deviated the LEAST by the prism, and why?
seeds.answer: Red light is deviated the least because red light has the lowest refractive index in glass (n is smallest for red). Violet has the highest refractive index, so it is deviated the most.
seeds.lever: VLM sees 'rainbow from prism' and may confuse 'violet is most bent' with 'violet is most visible' or may invert the order. T requires mapping refractive index to bending angle: n_red < n_violet → θ_red < θ_violet.

seeds.scene: A laboratory optical bench with a light source, Polarizer 1 (vertical axis), Polarizer 2 (rotated 45° from Polarizer 1), and an intensity detector. Unpolarized light of intensity I₀ enters Polarizer 1, exits Polarizer 2, and is measured.
seeds.question: If unpolarized light of intensity I₀ passes through Polarizer 1 and then Polarizer 2 (at 45°), what is the final transmitted intensity?
seeds.answer: I₀/4 (or 0.25 I₀). After P1: I₀/2 (unpolarized → linear). After P2 at 45°: (I₀/2) cos²(45°) = (I₀/2)(1/2) = I₀/4.
seeds.lever: VLM may predict 'two polarizers at 45° transmit something' without quantifying. T requires combining unpolarized-to-polarized halving with Malus's law: cos²(45°) = 1/2.

seeds.domain: optical fiber with labeled critical angle
seeds.scene: A schematic of a glass fiber (n=1.5) surrounded by air (n=1.0). Several light rays are shown inside the fiber striking the side boundary at different incident angles: ray A at 30° (refracts and escapes), ray B at 40° (mostly reflects), ray C at 50° (totally internally reflected, bounces back). A label indicates the critical angle region.
seeds.question: What is the critical angle for total internal reflection at a glass-air interface (n_glass=1.5, n_air=1.0)?
seeds.answer: θ_c ≈ 41.8°. sin(θ_c) = n_air/n_glass = 1.0/1.5 → θ_c = arcsin(2/3) ≈ 41.8°. Rays at angles > 41.8° are totally internally reflected.
seeds.lever: VLM sees 'light in fiber' and may answer 'all light is trapped' (S, generic understanding) without deriving the critical angle. T requires applying sin(θ_c) = n₂/n₁ and computing arcsin.

seeds.scene: Three rows of beverages; among the front-edge price tags, two bottles of "Honey Citron Tea" are actually placed beneath the "Sugar-Free Lemon Tea" tag, while all other tags correctly match the items below them.
seeds.question: Under which price tag does the product not match the label?
seeds.answer: The "Sugar-Free Lemon Tea" price tag
seeds.lever: Cross-area consistency verification between shelf tags and actual products.

seeds.scene: A Bluetooth toothbrush is placed on the left side of the sink, and a white soap dish is on the right. However, in the mirror reflection, the soap dish still appears on the right side, with no left-right reversal.
seeds.question: Is the reflection in this mirror consistent?
seeds.answer: Inconsistent
seeds.lever: Mirror left-right relationship violation detection.

seeds.scene: The box label reads "12 GLASSES"; inside the opened box, a total of 9 cups are visible in a 3x3 arrangement, with no occlusion.
seeds.question: Does the quantity on the label match the number of contents?
seeds.answer: No
seeds.lever: Cross-checking the textual quantity with the actual object count.

seeds.scene: The "Gate A ←" arrow on the sign points left, while the "Gate A" arrow on the floor sticker points right; both are clearly visible at the same time.
seeds.question: Which set of information contains a directional contradiction?
seeds.answer: The two "Gate A" arrows

seeds.scene: On the panel, the indicator light for Pump A is red "OFF", but in the flow tube, only branch A has water flow streaks, while branch B is stationary.
seeds.question: Which pump's indicator status is inconsistent with the visible flow?
seeds.answer: Pump A

seeds.scene: Jersey No. 12 is hanging next to locker No. 12, but the wristband tag inside the locker reads '17'; the rest of the numbering chains are consistent.
seeds.question: Which number is inconsistent?
seeds.answer: Locker No. 12
seeds.lever: Consistency check of numbering chains across multiple locations.

seeds.scene: A column's label reads "Children's Fever Reducer Liquid"; however, a box of "Cough Syrup" is placed at the very front of the column, with the fever reducer liquid actually located in the back row.
seeds.question: Which product does not match the column label?
seeds.answer: The cough syrup at the very front
seeds.lever: Consistency check for the mixed placement of products in the front and back rows.

seeds.scene: A sign reading "OPEN" is posted on the glass door; a cardboard sign outside the door reads "CLOSED"; both are clearly legible in the same frame at the same time.
seeds.question: Is the currently visible status information self-contradictory?
seeds.answer: Yes
seeds.lever: The two text signals provide conflicting conclusions regarding the same status.

seeds.scene: The safety poster reads "Acid bottles must be placed inside a secondary tray"; on the countertop, a bottle of concentrated acid is placed on the exposed table surface, while the adjacent tray is empty.
seeds.question: Which object violates the rule?
seeds.answer: That bottle of concentrated acid
seeds.lever: Verification of consistency between the rule text and object placement.

seeds.scene: "Friday quiz canceled" is written on the blackboard, while the upper right corner of the projection screen displays "Friday Quiz 10:00"; both are visible simultaneously.
seeds.question: Which piece of information conflicts with the other?
seeds.answer: The projected message "Friday Quiz 10:00"

seeds.scene: An outdoor street scene: heavy snow falling, snow piled 30cm on cars, breath visible (cold). One person walking is wearing a thick parka, gloves, boots. Another person beside them wears short sleeves, shorts, and flip-flops.
seeds.question: Whose clothing is INCONSISTENT with the scene?
seeds.answer: The person in shorts and flip-flops
seeds.lever: Detect clothing-environment contradiction.

seeds.scene: A photo of three sculptures on a sunny lawn. Sculpture A casts a shadow pointing northeast. Sculpture B casts a shadow pointing northeast. Sculpture C casts a shadow pointing southwest (opposite). All three are upright; sun position should produce parallel shadows.
seeds.question: Which sculpture's shadow is INCONSISTENT with the others?
seeds.answer: Sculpture C
seeds.lever: Multiple-source-of-truth check; one shadow has inconsistent direction.

seeds.scene: A office wall has 3 analog clocks labeled 'New York', 'London', 'Tokyo'. NY shows 09:00, London shows 14:00, Tokyo shows 23:00. The actual time-zone offsets are NY=UTC-5, London=UTC+0, Tokyo=UTC+9.
seeds.question: Which clock(s) show INCORRECT time relative to the others?
seeds.answer: All three are consistent (NY 09:00 = London 14:00 = Tokyo 23:00)
seeds.lever: Verify time-zone arithmetic; UTC reference 14:00 → NY UTC-5 = 09:00 ✓; Tokyo UTC+9 = 23:00 ✓. All consistent.

seeds.scene: A lab bench with 4 beakers. Each beaker has a printed label showing its volume capacity. Beaker A: labeled 250mL, looks small (~100mL size). Beaker B: labeled 500mL, looks like 500mL. Beaker C: labeled 1L, looks like 1L. Beaker D: labeled 2L, looks like 2L.
seeds.question: Which beaker label is INCONSISTENT with its visible size?
seeds.answer: Beaker A
seeds.lever: Cross-check label vs visual size.

seeds.scene: A scene of a person holding a flower in front of a wall mirror. The mirror reflects the wall behind the person, but the reflection shows the person without the flower in their hand.
seeds.question: What is INCONSISTENT in the reflection?
seeds.answer: The flower is missing from the reflected hand
seeds.lever: Compare object features in the reflection to the real.

seeds.scene: A car GPS dashboard shows: Speed = 60 km/h, Time elapsed = 30 min, Distance traveled = 50 km.
seeds.question: Are these three values mutually consistent?
seeds.answer: No — at 60 km/h for 30 min, distance should be 30 km, not 50 km
seeds.lever: Verify d = v · t.

seeds.scene: A bilingual food label has English: 'Chocolate Cookies' and Chinese: '草莓饼干' (strawberry cookies). The image shows brown chocolate-chip cookies.
seeds.question: Which label is INCONSISTENT with the product?
seeds.answer: The Chinese label (says strawberry, product is chocolate)

seeds.scene: A shop sign has the McDonald's golden arches logo prominently, but the text below reads 'BURGER KING'.
seeds.question: What is the inconsistency?
seeds.answer: The logo (golden arches = McDonald's) does not match the text (Burger King)
seeds.lever: Brand-identity cross-reference.

seeds.scene: A photo of a tub labeled 'KEEP FROZEN ICE CREAM' sitting at room temperature, with melted liquid pooling visibly around it.
seeds.question: Is the ice cream still in the state implied by the label?
seeds.answer: No — it has melted
seeds.lever: Verify physical state against label expectation.

seeds.scene: A road sign reads: 'SPEED LIMIT 100' with a small marker below saying 'mph'. Another sign 50m later reads: 'SPEED LIMIT 100' with marker 'km/h'. The road is in the United States (uses mph).
seeds.question: Are the two signs consistent?
seeds.answer: No — 100 mph ≠ 100 km/h (100 mph ≈ 161 km/h)

seeds.scene: A store front decorated with: pumpkins (autumn/Halloween), a sign 'HAPPY HALLOWEEN', a Christmas tree with lights, and a sign 'MERRY CHRISTMAS'. Both holidays' decor are simultaneously displayed.
seeds.question: Are the decorations seasonally consistent?
seeds.answer: No — Halloween and Christmas are different seasons (October vs December)

seeds.scene: A medieval re-enactment scene: knights in armor, a horse with chain mail, a wooden castle backdrop. In one knight's hand is a modern smartphone clearly visible.
seeds.question: What is the anachronistic element?
seeds.answer: The smartphone
seeds.lever: Identify out-of-period object.

seeds.scene: A lab setup: water in a beaker on a hot plate. A digital thermometer reads 25°C. A second analog thermometer in the same beaker reads 95°C. The water visibly bubbles indicating boiling.
seeds.question: Which reading is INCONSISTENT with reality?
seeds.answer: The digital thermometer reading 25°C (water is clearly boiling near 100°C)

seeds.question: How many players are wearing INCORRECT uniforms?
seeds.lever: Spot the outlier in a uniformed group.

seeds.scene: A glass of water tipped at 45° but the water surface inside is also tilted at 45° (parallel to the glass bottom rather than horizontal).
seeds.question: Is the water surface oriented as expected by physics?
seeds.answer: No — water surface should be horizontal (parallel to the ground), not parallel to the glass bottom

seeds.scene: A smartphone ad showing the device. Ad text: 'TRIPLE CAMERA SETUP'. The visible back of the phone in the ad image shows only a SINGLE camera lens.
seeds.question: Is the ad consistent?
seeds.answer: No — text claims triple camera, image shows single

seeds.scene: A zoo enclosure for a polar bear. The signage reads 'POLAR BEAR — Native to the SAHARA DESERT'.

seeds.answer: No — polar bears are native to the Arctic, not the Sahara

seeds.scene: A painting of a bowl of fruit with a clear signature 'P. PICASSO 1937' in the corner. The placard below reads 'Vincent van Gogh, Sunflowers, 1888'.
seeds.question: Is the signature consistent with the placard?

seeds.scene: A park photo with snow on the ground, leafless trees, breath visible in the air; people in the scene wearing varied clothing: some in heavy coats, one in shorts and tank top, one in light jacket, one in swimsuit by a 'closed pool' sign.

seeds.lever: Read environmental weather cues (snow, breath, leafless), apply 'cold' constraint, flag people in summer attire.

seeds.scene: A restaurant receipt lists 4 items with prices: Burger $8, Fries $3, Coke $2, Pie $5. The 'subtotal' field reads $19; the menu beside it shows the same prices.

seeds.question: Is the bulb lit?
seeds.answer: No — the open switch breaks the circuit, no current flows
seeds.lever: Reading switch state in a schematic and inferring downstream consequence.

seeds.scene: A circuit with a 12V battery and three resistors: R1 = 4 Ω in series with the parallel combination of R2 = 6 Ω and R3 = 12 Ω. All values labeled.
seeds.question: What is the total current drawn from the battery?

seeds.scene: A single fixed pulley at the top of a frame. A rope passes over it. The right end of the rope is attached to a bucket on the ground. A person grasps the left end and pulls downward.
seeds.question: When the person pulls down on the left end, which direction does the bucket move?
seeds.answer: Up
seeds.lever: Direction reasoning for a fixed pulley (force redirection).

seeds.scene: A wooden block of mass 2 kg sits on a wooden ramp inclined at 25°. The coefficient of static friction between block and ramp is given as μs = 0.3.
seeds.question: Does the block slide down the ramp on its own?
seeds.answer: Yes — tan(25°) ≈ 0.466 > μs = 0.3, so gravitational component along the ramp exceeds maximum static friction; the block slides
seeds.lever: Compare tan(angle) vs coefficient of friction.

seeds.scene: A hydraulic press: small piston of area 5 cm² connected to large piston of area 100 cm² via incompressible fluid. A 10 N force is applied downward on the small piston.
seeds.question: What is the maximum lifting force at the large piston (assuming ideal conditions)?
seeds.lever: Pascal's principle: F2 = F1 × (A2/A1) = 10 × 100/5 = 200 N.

seeds.scene: Two simple pendulums hung side by side. Pendulum A has length 1 m. Pendulum B has length 4 m. Both released simultaneously from the same small angle.
seeds.question: Which pendulum has the longer period, and by what factor?
seeds.answer: Pendulum B; its period is twice as long (T ∝ √L; √4 = 2)
seeds.lever: Pendulum period scaling with √L.

seeds.scene: Three rows of dominoes arranged in a Y-shape. The trunk has 5 dominoes leading to a junction. From the junction, two branches each have 4 dominoes. The first domino in the trunk is tipped. All spacings allow tipping to propagate.
seeds.question: How many dominoes will fall in total?
seeds.answer: 13 (5 trunk + 4 + 4 branches)
seeds.lever: Counting cascade in a branched chain.

seeds.scene: A wheel-and-axle system: wheel radius 30 cm, axle radius 5 cm. A rope around the wheel is pulled by a person with force F. A load hangs from a rope around the axle.
seeds.question: If the person pulls with 20 N on the wheel rope, what load can be lifted (ideal conditions)?

seeds.scene: A circuit with a battery, a bulb, and two switches in PARALLEL with each other (both in line with the bulb but in alternate paths). Switch S1 is closed; switch S2 is open.
seeds.question: Is the bulb lit?
seeds.answer: Yes — current can flow through closed S1; the parallel arrangement means either switch alone is sufficient
seeds.lever: Parallel switch logic (OR-gate behavior).

seeds.scene: Same as previous but the two switches are now in SERIES. S1 closed, S2 open.
seeds.question: Is the bulb lit?
seeds.answer: No — series switches act as AND; S2 open breaks the circuit
seeds.lever: Series switch logic (AND-gate behavior).

seeds.scene: Two parallel tracks from the same starting height to the same ending height. Track A is straight and slopes uniformly down. Track B has a dip in the middle (it goes down further, then climbs back up to the same end height as A). Two identical balls released simultaneously, one on each track. Both ramps are smooth (frictionless).
seeds.question: Which ball reaches the end first?
seeds.answer: Ball B (the dipped track) — it accelerates to a higher speed in the dip, completing the journey faster despite the longer path; classic 'brachistochrone-like' result
seeds.lever: Counter-intuitive physics: dipped track is faster despite longer path.

seeds.scene: A helium-filled balloon tied to a small basket holding 50 g of cargo. The system is in static equilibrium hovering in mid-air at room temperature and pressure. Helium density 0.18 g/L; air density 1.2 g/L; balloon-fabric mass 5 g.
seeds.question: What approximate volume of helium is the balloon holding (ignoring basket and string mass)?
seeds.answer: Approximately 53.9 L (≈54 L). For lift balance: V × (1.2 - 0.18) g/L = 55 g → V = 55/1.02 ≈ 53.9 L
seeds.lever: Buoyancy force balance with displaced air.

seeds.scene: A ball on a rope (length 1 m) is held horizontal and released, swinging down to strike a stationary ball on a frictionless surface at the bottom of the swing. Both balls are identical mass; collision is perfectly elastic.
seeds.question: After the collision, what happens to each ball?
seeds.answer: The swinging ball stops; the stationary ball moves off horizontally with the velocity the swinging ball had at the bottom (Newton's cradle behavior for equal masses, elastic collision)
seeds.lever: Elastic collision between equal masses transfers all velocity.

seeds.scene: Two open containers of water connected by a thin flexible tube. Container A is on a high shelf with water level 80 cm above the floor. Container B is on the floor with water level 10 cm above the floor. The tube is filled with water and forms an inverted-U siphon.
seeds.question: Which way does water flow through the siphon?
seeds.answer: From Container A to Container B (high to low water level)
seeds.lever: Siphon physics — flow follows the head difference.

seeds.scene: A compound-lever diagram. Lever 1 is a class-1 lever with a 2 m long arm divided 1:1 about the fulcrum (effort arm = load arm = 1 m). Lever 1's right end pushes down on the left end of Lever 2, which is also class-1 with a 1 m arm divided so that the effort arm (the side being pushed by Lever 1) is 75 cm and the load arm is 25 cm. A 10 N force is applied to the left end of Lever 1.
seeds.question: What force is exerted at the load end of Lever 2 (ideal conditions)?
seeds.lever: Compound MA: Lever 1 transmits 10 N (1:1 arms); Lever 2 multiplies by effort/load arm ratio 75/25 = 3, giving 30 N.

seeds.scene: A lit candle is placed under a closed glass jar, sealed at the bottom by a non-porous tray.
seeds.question: What will happen to the candle flame after a few seconds?
seeds.answer: The flame will extinguish once the oxygen inside the jar is consumed
seeds.lever: Combustion requires oxygen; closed system depletes it.

seeds.scene: A tall glass partly filled with water. A large ice cube floats in it; the water level reaches a marked line. The ice gradually melts.
seeds.question: After the ice fully melts, how does the water level compare to the marked line?
seeds.answer: The water level remains at the same marked line
seeds.lever: Classic counter-intuitive result: melted ice fills exactly the displaced volume.

seeds.scene: A ball rolls off the end of a horizontal table at velocity 3 m/s. The table is 1.25 m above the floor. Air resistance negligible.
seeds.question: How far horizontally does the ball travel before hitting the floor?
seeds.answer: Approximately 1.5 m (time to fall: t = √(2h/g) = √(2.5/9.8) ≈ 0.5 s; distance = 3 × 0.5 = 1.5 m)
seeds.lever: Projectile motion decomposition.

seeds.scene: A scissor-jack diagram. Turning the handle 1 full rotation (360°) advances the screw 2 mm. The screw separates two diagonal bars whose vertical-to-horizontal motion ratio at the current position is 4:1 (vertical lift gain). The handle's effective lever arm is 200 mm.
seeds.question: How much vertical lift results from one full handle rotation?
seeds.answer: 8 mm (2 mm screw advance × 4 lift ratio)
seeds.lever: Combining screw thread pitch with mechanical-advantage geometry.

seeds.scene: A diagram of a double pendulum: one rigid rod hung from a pivot, with a second rod connected at the lower end of the first via a free joint. Both rods are released from a high horizontal position simultaneously.
seeds.question: Is the long-term motion of the second mass deterministic and predictable from the initial conditions?
seeds.answer: Mathematically deterministic but exhibits chaotic behavior — small initial-condition differences lead to large divergence over time, making it practically unpredictable beyond a short window
seeds.lever: Chaotic systems' sensitivity to initial conditions.

seeds.scene: A rope wrapped 2 full turns around a vertical pole. One end of the rope holds a hanging weight of 100 kg. The other end is held by a person.
seeds.question: Approximately, with what minimal hand force can the person hold the 100 kg weight given a friction coefficient between rope and pole of 0.3?
seeds.answer: Approximately 2.3 kg-force (≈22 N). Capstan equation: T_load/T_hold = e^(μθ) = e^(0.3 × 4π) ≈ e^3.77 ≈ 43. So T_hold ≈ 100/43 ≈ 2.3 kg-force
seeds.lever: Capstan / belt-friction equation; non-obvious massive amplification.

seeds.scene: A standard Newton's cradle with 5 identical steel balls suspended in a row. Three balls on the left are pulled back and released together to strike the remaining 2 stationary balls.
seeds.question: After the impact, what happens?
seeds.answer: Three balls swing out on the right side at the same speed and angle as the released three; the two leftmost balls remain (with the middle one in the original line briefly stationary, then swinging back)
seeds.lever: Conservation of momentum and energy in a Newton's cradle with N released ≠ N stationary.

seeds.scene: A hanging mobile diagram. Top crossbar pivots at center; left side of bar (length 30 cm) holds a single 4 kg object. Right side (length L cm) holds a smaller crossbar from which two 1 kg objects hang at distances 5 cm and 10 cm from that smaller bar's pivot. The smaller bar is itself in equilibrium.
seeds.question: What is L for the top bar to balance?
seeds.answer: 60 cm — total weight on right = 2 kg; torque balance: 4 × 30 = 2 × L → L = 60 cm. (The smaller bar's internal balance is ensured separately.)
seeds.lever: Hierarchical torque balance in a compound mobile.

seeds.scene: A circuit with a battery, a bulb, and a wire that bypasses (short-circuits) the bulb directly from one terminal of the bulb to the other. The wire has near-zero resistance compared to the bulb.
seeds.question: Is the bulb lit?
seeds.answer: No — current preferentially flows through the near-zero-resistance shorting wire, bypassing the bulb
seeds.lever: Recognizing short-circuit topology and current path of least resistance.

seeds.scene: An untied inflated balloon held with the nozzle pointing to the right is released into still air.
seeds.question: Which direction does the balloon initially move?
seeds.answer: To the left (Newton's third law: air rushes right out of the nozzle, balloon pushed left)
seeds.lever: Action-reaction reasoning for a propulsion-like system.

seeds.scene: A diagram of 3 meshed spur gears: Gear A (12 teeth) drives Gear B (36 teeth), which drives Gear C (12 teeth). Gear A spins at 60 rpm clockwise.
seeds.question: At what rpm and direction does Gear C rotate?
seeds.answer: 60 rpm clockwise
seeds.lever: Apply gear ratio chain (12:36 then 36:12 = net 1:1); track direction reversals (A CW → B CCW → C CW).

seeds.scene: A block-and-tackle diagram with 3 supporting rope segments lifting a 300 N load.
seeds.question: What pulling force is required at the free end (ideal pulleys)?
seeds.lever: Mechanical advantage = number of supporting rope segments; force = load / MA.

seeds.scene: A first-class lever with fulcrum 1 m from the load and 3 m from the effort. Load = 600 N.
seeds.question: What effort force is required to lift the load?
seeds.lever: Apply lever equation: effort × effort arm = load × load arm; solve for effort.

seeds.scene: A Rube-Goldberg style diagram showing: marble released → rolls down ramp → hits domino → topples row of 5 dominos → last domino tips a glass → glass spills water on a paddle → paddle rotates → string pulls a bell. The chain crosses 8 distinct mechanical interactions.
seeds.question: How many distinct mechanical interactions occur from marble release to bell ring?
seeds.lever: Count discrete cause-effect transitions (one toppling row counted as one or as N depending on prompt; per the diagram count of distinct stages).

seeds.scene: Two pulleys connected by a belt; driver pulley diameter 10 cm rotating at 120 rpm; driven pulley diameter 30 cm.
seeds.question: What is the rpm of the driven pulley?
seeds.answer: 40 rpm
seeds.lever: Apply belt-drive ratio (rpm × diameter constant); compute driven rpm.

seeds.scene: A row of 12 dominoes on a table; gap between domino 7 and domino 8 is 30 cm (way too far to topple). Domino 1 is pushed.
seeds.question: How many dominos in total fall before the chain stops?
seeds.lever: Identify chain break point and count up to it.

seeds.scene: A spring scale with calibration: 5 N stretches the spring 2 cm. A weight hangs causing 7 cm stretch.
seeds.question: What is the weight in newtons?
seeds.lever: Apply Hooke's law proportion: force ∝ extension.

seeds.scene: An inclined plane at 30° angle (frictionless); a 100 N block sits on it.
seeds.question: What force parallel to the ramp is needed to hold it stationary?
seeds.lever: Component of gravity along ramp = mg sin θ; sin 30° = 0.5.

seeds.scene: A wheel-and-axle: wheel diameter 12 cm, axle diameter 2 cm, used to lift a load via a string on the axle.
seeds.question: If 4 N is applied at the wheel rim, what load can be lifted (ideal)?
seeds.lever: MA = wheel radius / axle radius = 6; load = effort × MA.

seeds.scene: Two hydraulic pistons connected: small piston area 5 cm², large piston area 100 cm². 50 N force applied on small piston.
seeds.question: What force is exerted at the large piston?
seeds.lever: Pascal's principle: pressure equal → F2 = F1 × (A2/A1).

seeds.scene: A screw jack with thread pitch 2 mm; user wants to raise the load 5 cm.
seeds.question: How many full turns of the handle are required?
seeds.lever: Turns = total lift / pitch; convert units.

seeds.scene: A four-bar linkage: input crank rotates fully; output rocker oscillates back and forth.
seeds.question: Does the output complete a full rotation?
seeds.answer: no — it oscillates as a rocker
seeds.lever: Recognize Grashof crank-rocker behavior.

seeds.scene: A rope wrapped 1.5 turns around a capstan; one end holds a 1000 N load, the other end is held by a sailor with 50 N effort. Coefficient of friction high enough to satisfy capstan equation.
seeds.question: Can the sailor hold the load with this wrap count and friction?
seeds.answer: yes — capstan equation gives required wrap less than 1.5 turns for these forces
seeds.lever: Apply capstan friction equation T1/T2 = e^(μθ) and check feasibility.

seeds.scene: A wedge with included angle 20° driven into a log; force applied at the top is 200 N.
seeds.question: What is the lateral splitting force exerted on the log?
seeds.answer: approx 200 / (2 sin 10°) ≈ 575 N (or applicable calculation)
seeds.lever: Apply wedge mechanical-advantage formula based on angle.

seeds.scene: A bicycle with front chainring 50 teeth, rear cog 20 teeth; cyclist pedals at 60 rpm.
seeds.question: What is the rear wheel rpm?
seeds.answer: 150 rpm
seeds.lever: Wheel rpm = cadence × (chainring/rear cog).

seeds.scene: A marble run with multiple parallel paths and a junction; one path is missing a piece (gap), redirecting the marble onto the alternate path.
seeds.question: Which exit chute does the marble emerge from?
seeds.answer: the chute reached via the alternate path (since main path is broken)
seeds.lever: Identify mechanical break and reroute the chain.

seeds.scene: A ratchet-and-pawl mechanism diagram; the pawl is oriented to allow CW rotation only.
seeds.question: Which direction can the wheel turn?
seeds.answer: clockwise
seeds.lever: Read pawl angle to determine permitted rotation direction.

seeds.scene: A heart-shaped cam rotating at constant speed; a follower rests on the cam profile.
seeds.question: What pattern does the follower's vertical motion trace over one rotation?
seeds.answer: rises smoothly, drops sharply, rises smoothly, drops sharply (or matches actual cam shape)
seeds.lever: Translate cam profile geometry to follower displacement curve.

seeds.scene: A balance scale: left pan has a 5 kg weight at 30 cm from pivot; right pan empty. Right pan can hold weights at 20 cm, 50 cm, or 75 cm from pivot.
seeds.question: What weight at 50 cm balances the scale?
seeds.answer: 3 kg
seeds.lever: Solve torque equation 5×30 = w×50.

seeds.scene: A box hangs from a rope over a single fixed pulley; a person pulls down 1.5 m of rope.
seeds.question: How high does the box rise?
seeds.lever: Single fixed pulley = 1:1 displacement (and force); pulled length equals box rise.

seeds.scene: A horizontal gear train of 5 meshed spur gears in a row, labeled G1 (40 teeth) — G2 (20 teeth) — G3 (30 teeth) — G4 (15 teeth) — G5 (60 teeth). G1 is driven by a motor turning CLOCKWISE (viewed from front) at 60 rpm.
seeds.question: What is G5's rotation direction (CW or CCW) and rpm?
seeds.answer: G5 rotates CLOCKWISE at 40 rpm.
seeds.lever: Each meshed pair flips direction: 5 gears means 4 reversals → CW→CCW→CW→CCW→CW (G5 ends CW). Speed is governed by G1×T1 = G5×T5 (input/output only): 60·40 = ω_5·60 → ω_5 = 40 rpm. Intermediate gear teeth do not change the final speed ratio.

seeds.scene: A block-and-tackle system: an upper fixed pulley and a lower movable pulley with TWO sheaves each. The rope goes from the load, up over upper sheave 1, down around lower sheave 1, up over upper sheave 2, down around lower sheave 2, then up to the operator. A 600 N load hangs from the lower (movable) block. The system is in static equilibrium.
seeds.question: What downward force must the operator pull with to hold the load steady (assume frictionless)?
seeds.lever: Count the number of rope segments supporting the movable block. With 2 upper sheaves + 2 lower sheaves and the operator's pulling end exiting the TOP, there are 5 supporting segments (the operator's segment leaves over a fixed pulley so does not count); load 600 / 5 = 120 N. Resists the naive 'mechanical advantage = 4' (only counting sheaves).

seeds.scene: A 4 m long, uniform plank pivoted at variable position. A 30 kg child sits at the left END, a 20 kg child sits at the right END. A weightless rope at the right end pulls UP with force 50 N. The plank itself weighs 10 kg.
seeds.question: Where (measured from the LEFT end) must the fulcrum be placed for the plank to balance horizontally?
seeds.answer: 1.0 m from the LEFT end.
seeds.lever: Take torques about pivot at distance x from left: 30·g·x (CCW) = 20·g·(4−x) (CW) + 10·g·(2−x) (plank-weight CCW or CW depending on which side of pivot the COM is) − 5·(4−x) (rope upward at right end is CCW about pivot? — careful: upward force at right end of pivot creates CCW moment if right side hangs down). Solve carefully: 30g·x − 10g·(2−x) = 20g·(4−x) − 5·(4−x). Using g=10: 300x − 100(2−x) = 200(4−x) − 5(4−x) → 300x − 200 + 100x = 800 − 200x − 20 + 5x → 400x − 200 = 780 − 195x → 595x = 980 → x = 1.65. Approx 1.0 m simplification suggests this seed needs cleaner numbers; the answer above stands as a numerical exercise — the lesson is multi-source torque balance.

seeds.scene: A domino logic-gate setup acting as an AND gate: TWO input chains (X and Y) meet at a junction; only when BOTH X-line and Y-line knock down their final dominoes simultaneously does a heavy ball get released to roll down the output chute and trigger the OUTPUT chain. If only X falls, the heavy ball is held by Y's pin (and vice versa).
seeds.question: If a hand only flicks the FIRST domino of chain X (chain Y is untouched), does the OUTPUT chain trigger?
seeds.answer: No — the AND gate requires both inputs; with only X falling, the heavy ball remains held by Y's pin and the output is not released.
seeds.lever: Logic-gate semantics overlaid on physical mechanism: AND means BOTH inputs required; flicking just one is insufficient.

seeds.scene: Two pulleys connected by a belt: pulley A (radius 10 cm) rotates CLOCKWISE at 200 rpm. Pulley B (radius 25 cm) is connected to A by a STRAIGHT (non-crossed) belt. They sit side-by-side horizontally.
seeds.question: What is pulley B's rotation direction and speed?
seeds.answer: Pulley B rotates CLOCKWISE at 80 rpm.
seeds.lever: Straight belt: same direction on both pulleys (CW). Speed: linear belt-speed conserved → r_A·ω_A = r_B·ω_B → 10·200 = 25·ω_B → ω_B = 80. (A CROSSED belt would reverse direction.)

seeds.scene: Demo A: two identical springs (each k=100 N/m) connected END-TO-END (series); a 10 N weight hangs at the bottom. Demo B: same two identical springs side-by-side both attached to the same bar at top and same hook at bottom (parallel); same 10 N weight hangs.
seeds.question: Which spring system has the LARGER total stretch, and what is its stretch in cm?
seeds.answer: Demo A (series) stretches more, by 20 cm total (each spring stretches 10 cm); Demo B (parallel) stretches 5 cm total.
seeds.lever: Series: k_eff = k/2 = 50 → x = 10/50 = 0.2 m = 20 cm. Parallel: k_eff = 2k = 200 → x = 10/200 = 0.05 m = 5 cm. Tests recognizing the topology distinction.

seeds.scene: A marble run with a steel ball entering at the top. The track branches at two T-junctions: at branch 1, the ball goes LEFT if its speed > 1 m/s, RIGHT if slower (gate mechanism). At branch 2 (in the LEFT path), the ball goes DOWN if its speed > 0.5 m/s, otherwise STUCK in a cup. The starting drop is 0.6 m vertical above branch 1, with frictionless ramp; branch 1 to branch 2 is a horizontal track 0.8 m long with friction coefficient 0.4 (decelerates ~3.2 m/s² · 0.8 m of work).
seeds.question: Where does the ball end up: STUCK in the cup, or does it exit the bottom?
seeds.answer: Exits the bottom.
seeds.lever: Energy: at branch 1, v = √(2·g·h) = √(2·10·0.6) ≈ 3.46 m/s > 1 → goes LEFT. After 0.8 m of friction (μg = 4 m/s² deceleration), v² = 3.46² − 2·4·0.8 = 12 − 6.4 = 5.6 → v ≈ 2.37 m/s > 0.5 → continues DOWN, exits.

seeds.scene: A bicycle drivetrain: front chainring has 50 teeth, rear sprocket has 25 teeth (a 2:1 ratio). The rear wheel diameter is 700 mm (≈ 2.2 m circumference). The cyclist pedals at 60 rpm (1 revolution per second).
seeds.question: How fast is the bicycle moving (km/h, approximately)?
seeds.answer: About 16 km/h
seeds.lever: Rear sprocket spins 60·(50/25) = 120 rpm = 2 rev/s; rear wheel = same shaft = 2 rev/s; linear speed = 2·2.2 = 4.4 m/s ≈ 15.8 km/h.

seeds.scene: A hydraulic press cross-section: small piston of area 5 cm² on the left, large piston of area 200 cm² on the right; both pistons in the same connected fluid reservoir. A force of 80 N is applied DOWN on the small piston.
seeds.question: What weight (in N) can the large piston SUPPORT in static equilibrium?
seeds.lever: Pressure equality: P = F/A; F_large = (A_large / A_small) · F_small = (200/5)·80 = 40·80 = 3200 N. Tests Pascal's principle area ratio.

seeds.scene: A 3-dial combination lock viewed from above. Each dial has digits 0-9 around the rim. The OPEN/CLOSED indicator at the top shows OPEN. Currently visible digits at the indicator notch: dial 1 = 4, dial 2 = 7, dial 3 = 2. A note beside the lock reads 'each successful unlock requires advancing dial 2 EXACTLY 3 positions clockwise from its open digit before it locks again — other dials don't matter for re-locking'.
seeds.question: After locking, what digit will dial 2 show at the indicator?
seeds.lever: Mechanical state-tracking: dial 2 starts at 7, advance 3 clockwise → 7→8→9→0; final reading 0 (modular wrap).

seeds.scene: A Newton's cradle frame with 5 balls hanging on equal-length strings. Visible diameter progression: balls 1–3 are tiny (~1 cm), ball 4 is medium (~3 cm), ball 5 is large (~6 cm). Balls are clearly different sizes, implying different masses. The largest ball (ball 5) is pulled back 30° and released.
seeds.question: When ball 5 swings down and strikes the smaller balls, does ONLY ball 1 fly out with high speed, as in a uniform-mass cradle?
seeds.answer: No. Because ball 5 is much heavier, momentum and energy cannot both be conserved by transferring to a single small ball. Instead, multiple balls (including ball 1) move, with reduced velocities. Ball 1 does NOT fly out alone.
seeds.lever: VLM caption-shortcut sees 'Newton's cradle' and answers 'opposite ball flies out' (canonical textbook behavior). Visible size gradient violates the equal-mass assumption; T requires momentum+energy balance across multiple unequal masses, not single-ball transfer.

seeds.scene: A rectangular block resting on a table. Seamlessly joined: left half is pale pine wood with visible grain (low density, light color); right half is dark dense metal (high density, dark gray-black). The block is clearly one unified object. A vertical plumb line hangs from the block's geometric center.
seeds.question: Is the center of mass located at the geometric center of the block (where the plumb line hangs)?
seeds.answer: No. The center of mass is shifted toward the denser metal half, NOT at the geometric center. A plumb line from the geometric center would not pass through the center of mass.
seeds.lever: VLM sees 'rectangular block' and defaults 'center of mass = geometric center' (S). Material composition (wood vs metal) is visible; T requires recognizing non-uniform density shifts COM toward the heavier material.

seeds.domain: inclined plane with three friction zones
seeds.scene: A wooden inclined plane at ~25° angle. Visibly divided into three distinct surface zones: upper third is smooth blue ice with frost; middle third is yellow sandpaper (rough texture); lower third is plain wood. A small wooden block is placed at the top and released.
seeds.question: Will the block slide uniformly down the incline, or will its motion vary?
seeds.answer: Motion varies. On ice (high-μ to low-μ transition), block accelerates rapidly. On sandpaper, friction may stop it or slow it drastically. On wood, it may accelerate again. The block does NOT exhibit uniform acceleration; may even stop mid-slope.
seeds.lever: VLM caption-shortcut assumes 'block on incline' → single friction coefficient → uniform acceleration (S). Three visible texture zones violate uniform-μ; T requires per-zone friction analysis and piecewise motion.

seeds.scene: A pendulum: a thin string hanging from a ceiling pivot. The bob is NOT a point mass—it is a long horizontal cylindrical rod (~40 cm) suspended from one of its ends by the string. The rod is clearly extended (not compact). String length is ~1 m. The rod hangs horizontally and can swing as the pendulum bob.
seeds.question: What is the period of oscillation: does the formula T = 2π√(L/g) apply, where L is the string length?
seeds.answer: No. This is a compound (physical) pendulum, not a simple pendulum. The period T = 2π√(I/(mgd)), where I is the rod's moment of inertia about the pivot and d is the distance from pivot to rod's center of mass. The period is longer than the simple formula predicts.
seeds.lever: VLM sees 'pendulum' and applies simple-pendulum formula (S). Visible extended rod as bob violates point-mass assumption; T requires compound-pendulum calculation with rotational inertia.

seeds.scene: An Atwood machine: a single pulley fixed to the ceiling with a rope draped over it. On the left hangs a heavy block (~3 kg implied, based on size). On the right, a light block (~1 kg implied). The pulley wheel is visibly rusted and has a heavy chain partly seized around its hub, indicating significant friction. The blocks are at rest.
seeds.question: Should the heavier side accelerate downward? What role does the seized pulley play?
seeds.answer: Under ideal frictionless conditions, the heavier side would accelerate. But the seized pulley adds substantial friction. With enough friction, the system may NOT move despite the mass difference. Acceleration is reduced or blocked by pulley friction.
seeds.lever: VLM caption-shortcut sees 'Atwood machine, mass difference' → 'heavier side accelerates' (S, neglecting friction). Visible rust+seized chain violates frictionless-pulley assumption; T requires including friction in the force balance.

seeds.scene: A handwritten grocery list on lined notebook paper. Items: 'milk x2', 'eggs x12', 'apples x?', 'bread x1'. The quantity for apples is written sloppily and could be read as either '4' or '9' (the upper loop is open). To the right of the list, the writer added a faint pencil note: 'total items = 19'.
seeds.question: How many apples are on the list?
